review_text:
A.k.a. Xiao La Jiao, this basement restaurant has great Szechuan food.  My particular favorite is the lamb with cumin and Szechuan peppercorns.    The cumin and chili powder-laced french fries are also pretty unique. Other good dishes are cold noodles, ma po tofu, dan dan noodles,  twice cooked pork, and pig's ear.  Best Szechuan around, IMHO.

It's authentic, so it's very spicy and has the unique taste of Szechuan peppercorns.   And some of the dishes can be fairly oily, swimming in brilliant red colored chili oil.  They also have more unusual dishes available: lamb, frog and rabbit.

Oh Little Pepper--I'm so sorry. I can only give you four stars. I was actually going to give you three but I had a flavor flashback of your beautiful lamb in spicy cumin and bumped you up one.

Yesterday three friends and I took the long, long ride out on the seven train to Flushing with one goal in mind--Little. Pepper. I had been here once before, about a year ago.

Now this is a very important part of the story, so listen up. When I came here the first time, I hadn't been to any other Sichuan places. And this wonderfully masochistic spicy dinner blew my mind and my scalp was sweating all night. (my sister gets the nose-sweats, I get the scalp...same root--pepper oil) But since last June, I've been a regular customer at Grand Sichuan down on Canal. And I think it corrupted me.

You know how it's hard to go back to Jim Beam when you've been drinking Johnny Walker Black for the last year? Well, it's kinda like that. Little Pepper is just Jim Beam next to Grand Sichuan's Johnny...but you still get the spicy aftershocks the next day, regardless of quality.

Yes, I was a bit disappointed last night. The pork with crispy rice cake was not very good. In fact the meat tasted like that weird unidentifiable rubber you get at Panda Express. The wontons in spicy oil were quite good, but, again, I'm crying for you Little Pepper, they paled in comparison to Grand Sichuan's. Even the cucumber with mashed garlic didn't seem as fresh as it could have been. And cucumber always seems fresh.

So you're probably wondering why the hell I rated this place four stars. Well, it's almost exclusively for the lamb in spicy sauce (with cumin). You will find it identified on the menu as such. It is really great. The taste actually hints at lamb halal street meat, but it's better since it's not some weird compressed meatloaf that's been gyrating all day exposed to the elements. It's real meat, and the difference here is a light sifting of sichuan peppercorns on top.

We tried to get the rabbit (and my friend was lobbying for bullfrog) but they were out of rabbit and we were feeling more like comfort food than experimentation so we didn't try either.

When all is said and done, I don't know if I'm coming back to you, Little Pepper. I may just save myself the $4 and the long train ride and venture down to that little smoky hole-in-the-wall on Canal. I won't rub it in again by saying its name. Sorry.

((Oh--and LP--one more thing before it's over. Don't tone down the spice for the out-of-towners. The spice factor in your food left us wanting more...we don't go to sichuan for fun. We go for serious capsaicin comas. You just didn't deliver.))

Little Mr. Pepper,  I really wanted to five star you just because I eat your food so often.  

True, the cumin lamb is a great dish, but the fries may show off the interplay of cumin and red chili powder even better.  For me, your best dish is the shrimp with hot and spicy sauce because when you're on, no other dish has as much nuance and complexity.  

But you can be inconsistent.  Sometimes, the red oil leafy tripe is just too salty.  Or there's not enough sichuan peppercorn in the husband wife.  But that won't stop me from coming in tonight and getting a container of ma la tendon, an order of water-cooked fish fillets, and that shrimp.  And a container of beef jerky that I can pick at until all that's left is the red oil-slicked bottom of a plastic takeout container.  Some people might walk across the street and get their Sichuan fix at Spicy and Tasty, but really, why bother.  They've got nothing on you, Mr. Pepper.

Extremely solid Szechuan food. Ironically their best dishes aren't even 100% native Szechuan versions, the noodles in spicy brown sauce with beef felt more Taiwanese (but oh so yummy once mixed up), and the cold cucumber with garlic... mmmm, just the right amount of crunch and large amounts of garlic.

We also had the pork intestine that was perfectly chewy and seasoned, although it wasn't spicy at all. That might have been my biggest issue-- dishes that were supposed to be spicy really weren't that spicy. It's probably a nice blend of spice level, though, so you don't scare the unwashed masses away. It is also distinctly possible that I enjoy spicy food way too much and that's why the heat barely registered...

And for a little basement hole in the wall, the charm is just about right.

The best hot pot place in flushing. Their plates come in big serving and are very fresh. Some dishes such as beef inner stomach can't be found in any other hot pot places. 

If you're looking for a spotlessly clean place, go somewhere else.

3.565 stars

I'm feeling that Taiwanese/Szechuan fusion vibe here others mentioned. We tried some staples like the Cold Spicy Beef Tendon, thin sliced and creamy in texture, with the hard high fastball heat (spiciness). That was possibly the best dish we sampled. Although not on the menu in the Braised Section they made the dish with thin sliced pork for us, you can get it with pork intestine too, but having had chitlens early in the week in Boston we opted for just the pork. We had a split decision on the Pork with Dry Bean Curd, I thought it was quite good  but the cut of pork was quite fatty. For the veggie we tried the Napa Cabbage with Dried Pepper Szechuan Style. It was not quite spicy enough for me and I found myself dunking the cabbage in the Braised pork sauce, which did enhance the flavor. If this place was in Massachusetts it would be in the top 3 Szechuan establishments, in Flushing, they need to keep pace a little better. The staff was very friendly and helpful and that does count for something. Xiao La Jiao deserves a 2nd, and probably 3rd visit before final judgement.

* I'm a sucker for basement venues, my first apartment was subterranean.
* Prices have risen significantly, about 30% but that's a sign of the times 
I suppose.
* Wide and deep offerings should be something for every spicy food lover.
* they didn't have rabbit this visit

Quite good Sichuan food.  The chong qing spicy chicken (la zi ji) is outstanding, definitely try that.  The water-cooked spicy beef (shui zhu niu) is decent, but not as good as at some of the other Sichuan places around NY like Sichuan Gourmet.  Also, not much (i.e. nothing) in the way of ambiance.

Definitely enjoyable, but not worth the trip out to Flushing versus the Manhattan Sichuan places.  I do want to come back and try the hot pot here though.

I spent a summer in China and I thought I would never again feel the delicious sting of being bitch-slapped by Sichuan cuisine- and then I discovered Little Pepper.  I am no expert but man this food is spicy and yummy and CHEAP.

I recommend the braised fish in spicy soup base, homemade pork dumplings, homemade tofu, and the lotus root with chilis (the dry one- the one with sauce is a little too cloying).  I can not emphasize how delicious fresh tofu is with some chili oil and boiled peanuts and scallions.  If you've only ever had that brick deep fried and covered in sticky sweet chili sauce you need to try the real thing.  And in case you have any reservations about the fish- I can honestly say that it is some of the freshest I've had in all of NYC.  Lotus root is pretty much a more interesting potato.  I like it's subtle flavor and crunch even after being cooked.  If you haven't had it before give it a try.

I can't speak for every dish on the menu but the ones I mentioned are all winners. I only wish that I could get bigger groups of people to go with me so I could do the hot pot or order about ten other things.

P.S.  Most of the time the servers don't speak English but I've never had a problem just pointing and smiling.  If you're a stickler for service this is not your place- I usually just help myself to a second beer from the cooler

This place is super dumpy but it doesn't matter. The beautiful pepper is all I need to see. I haven't eaten here in a while, but it's good. Go for the hot pot. Nowhere in Manhattan compares with Sichuan places in Flushing. Please. Do not speak if all you have to say is nonsense.

Down the stairs we went, following the peppers in the window. Our waiter boasted of the chefs talents and of the braised fish dish that had been written up in the NY Times. He was not wrong. The flakey swai fish was amazing in a fiery pot of broth. We also ordered the wood ear mushrooms and pork. I would also highly recommend this dish, the funky looking mushrooms and pork came together with layered flavors and a kick of spice.  The kitchen did a good job at toning down the spice for us, though there was enough to provide that szechuan mouth burn.  

Note: they are moving in 3 months to 18-24 College Point Blvd
bigger location apparently, but that will be a big loss for this neighborhood

This is one of those places that makes you so very happy you know about it. The sign is chinese with a friendly cartoon pepper. It's down some stairs. It's tiny. The food is great. I've been a few times now and it's consistently great, which is even better. They've yet to serve me something average. They serve beer.

Be advised, the entree portions are pretty big. Of course, you should still order as if it's your last meal, as the food is so solid. Take the leftovers home, wake up the next morning, make some fresh rice and enjoy round two.

You need to try the pork dumplings in hot sauce. SO damn good. I'm a fan of the Smoked pork with leeks as well. The spicy chicken dish mentioned in an earlier review was the winner of the first meal I had here, which, considering it's chicken, is something of an accomplishment.

As an added bonus it's south of the 7 station so you avoid the crowds if you're not in the mood to deal.
Spicy cumin lamb and scallion fried rice. And cold beer. Go there and eat it.

I have been frequenting Little Pepper for several weeks (often) and have to say I'm a huge fan.

Not pretentious in the least.  People are nice, food is awesome, portions are good size, beer is cold and cheap.  What the hell else do I need?....

The first few visits I thought the food could be a bit spicier, but now that they have seen us a few times, the heat is definitely there.  

Some favorites (so far):
- Cucumber in Mashed Garlic Sauce (I'm a big pickle fan)
- Spicy Lamb with Cumin (tops)
- Pork Dumplings
- Braised Sliced Fish in Spicy Soup

Rabbit and Bullfrog are next up for me to try.

All hail the Pepper!!!

Confused about entering this place, it actually is downstairs. A basement restaurant, interesting. Following my foodie cravings, I wanted to check this place out for myself.

We obviously had to go for the spicy cumin lamb that everyone seems to suggest. Not killer spicy, but still left me sweating. Served with sauteed onions, people are right that it's a must order. The lamb is fatty and delicious. My only complaint is that it's a bit oily.
Then the cauliflower and pork. A decent dish, definitely helped by the thinly sliced fatty pork.
To add onto the weight, we also had Chinese sausage and leeks. If you've never had Chinese sausage, try this out. It's smoky and probably different from most sausages that you've tried (that's what she said.) Leeks went very well with the dish, but again, a bit too oily.

In the end, the three of us were pretty stuffed from the three dishes and even had a little bit to take home. A good meal, but not the cheapest when you're in this area ($15 a person with tax/tip).

Little Pepper (or Xiao La Jiao) is a misnomer.  They might be small tiny particles of crushed peppers and spices, but they don't just put a little on their Szechuan dishes.  They load them with lots and lots of pepper.  I speak of one dish in particular, but this cuisine as a whole is not for the little of stomach.

I had been to this basement restaurant in Flushing a few years ago and I remember that it was the first time I had a crazy sensation from spicy food.  What happened was this:  The spice (I think particularly the Szechuan peppers) was so overwhelming that when I drank tap water, it felt like it was carbonated.  My taste buds had actually gone numb.  I felt like I was on some sort of drug.  It was both a very neat and alarming sensation.  I had the same experience when I returned to Flushing a few years later and ate at the Golden Mall.  I think I had a chili rabbit dish both times.

As tempted as I was to try a little sparkling tap water again,we skipped the rabbit and instead ordered the much-publicized Lamb with Hot and Spicy Sauce (with Cumin).  When this finally came to the table, wrapped in aluminum foil, the overwhelming aroma of cumin filled my nose, my mouth, my eyes.  It was really intense.  I generally like cumin but it felt like I had fallen into a vat of cumin quick sand.

I could also see the meat was covered with tons of crushed red peppers and a garnish of cilantro.  I took maybe two bites and didn't get much lamb flavor.  I only got heat.  Lots of heat.  And I found myself crunching on what felt like seeds but I knew were those pepper flakes.  They were attacking my mouth like an army of fire ants.  And the charming non-English speaking staff were too busy to refill my water.

I wanted to like this, but truth be told, I couldn't finish it.  I could barely get a quarter of the dish ingested.  And the lack of balance to me really turned me off.  I was surprised that this dish is so well-received all over the internet.  I guess some people have bionic taste buds.

We got a few other dishes (which we had to order by pointing to because of the language barrier) and they fared a little better.  The pork dumplings in soup were sort of the opposite of the cumin lamb. They had no flavor at all (or had my tastebuds all been destroyed?) and tasted like bland wontons.  The Chinese broccoli helped cool the heat a bit - even though I could see some Szechuan peppers hiding among the green.  But the Spicy Sichuan Cold Noodles were the winner.  They definitely had quite a bit of heat, but were balanced well with a touch of cold savory sweetness.

I am pleased to inform you all that my tastebuds have since recovered and I think I will still be able to taste and write Yelp reviews.  It was a close one there.

-eatthisny

Wow-- came here on a whim after reading all the raving reviews here. The food burns so good. 
Had:  Cold spicy chicken appetizer, $7.95- pretty good sized dish with chilli oil, peanuts, scallions, cilantro, sesame, sichuan peppercorns-- spicy and great on rice
Cumin lamb, $13.95- bite sized pieces of tender lamb with cilantro and onion, very tasty and smelled like roofer armpits
Cumin crab, $11.95- 4 whole crabs with a lot of spice! eating this was so delicious and messy! 
Note: 2 people with plenty of leftovers

Overall, really enjoyed the meal. It was very good. Everything was obviously spicy, but never overpowered the flavor. My taste buds weren't overloaded on heat, but my body started to perspire somewhat & my sinuses cleared.

After reading about it in T Magazine, I have to say I regret not trying the 'Crusts of cooked rice with pork' and I will definitely be going back to have that.

4.5... 
0.5 for improvement.. that said.. i seldom have craving for it's mala fish!  
Mala fish is in a big metal pot with vegetable (mushroom etc) on bottom and fish on top, inside this spicy soup/oil... it's awesome!  Fish is so tender, very tasty and the hotness doesn't kill the taste!

The boss is very nice, if she knows you are first timer there, she'd introduce you their specialties, and you should trust her!  She's the only lady waitress there...

This is some next-level Szechuan food. I'd rate it above Spicy & Tasty and Grand Sichuan; the location and crowd are also refreshingly low-key and authentic. Top dish was the Chongqing-style spicy chicken. The enhanced salt&pepper pork seemed an awful lot like double-cooked pork but was very tasty so we didn't mind. And the shredded stir-fried eggplant was pungent and delicious. We'll definitely return soon.

I love this place!  The food is beautifully spicy and the Tsingtaos are only $2.  My favorite dishes are the lotus root with dry pepper, the spicy fries and the pork with sweet bean sauce.  Based on yelp recommendations, I'll have to try the lamb with cumin next time I visit Little Pepper.  The basement location is not luxurious, but it is comfy and unpretentious.

I've been coming here periodically for the last two years, first introduced by a Chinese friend and now I can drag my coworkers here too!  This place is authentic and spicy and NOT for the faint of heart. 

The staff are friendly and the proprietress has always been great in suggesting other dishes we should try. I'm illiterate in Chinese and can only manage a few words, but they're really patient to make sure you enjoy the meal. (I've even had to pull out my iPhone to show them pictures of the dishes I wanted.)  I'd come out a lot more if Flushing wasn't 2 hours away from WashHts ...

My reliable dishes:
- ma la yu / shui zhu yu - both are braised fish filets in spicy chili oil. The first dish is larger and also includes bean sprouts and tofu (?) slices. Careful of the Sichuan peppercorns, they're seriously tongue-numbing.
- sauteed cowpeas with minced pork - tangy pickled string beans with juicy bits of meat. Occasionally a little over-salted, but hands-down my favorite thing to spoon over rice and chow down on.
- sichuan liang mien (sichuan cold noodles) - tangy, cold, vinegary, peanuty noodles. mmm.

I've also stopped in for takeout and they're super-speedy about it, less than 10 minutes waiting for two noodle dishes and one vegetable.

A tip for combating the spiciness: if water and beer don't do it for you, make a stop for milk tea boba at Ten Ren (half a block east) before heading in. It does wonders.

If this restaurant is in China it would just be another below average joint you run into on the block. But then again we are talking about flushing and it surely is glorified by americanized taste buds. I will explain why Little Pepper and me dont see eye to eye..

Came here on a hot satruday afternoon and found this place. 
The AC is literally non-existent. Although its a small restaurant holding about 6 tables, they only had 2 waiters juggling between tables and the customers waiting for tables. Needless to say our service was SLOW. She was apologetic though. 

Anyways we ordered 4 dishes - wayyyyyy too much food for 2 people. 

Cuming Lamb -  The flavor of the lamb is totally lost in the spice, It is spicy I assure you that, is just that underneath the spice and cuming there isn't much substance to it. 

Saliva chicken - I'm not sure if there is an english name for this dish as it literally translates to Saliva chicken. The portion is impressive. the meat is tender. It's just a little sweet for my taste. I have ordered this dish countless times whenever I go to a sichuan restaurant, and this is the first time I've had it sweet. It's spicy and had layers of flavors, its just the sweetness I can't get over. 

fried pepper - Not sure if this is the exact name for the dish. But its pepper deep fried and pan fried. The flavor is right on but they left the seed in the pepper... which totally ruined the texture and the left a bad after taste in my mouth.

Water boiled beef - This is where shit hit the fan. No matter how much seasoning and pepper you put into that dish you just can't mask bad beef. The beef smelled foul and tasted sour. It was subtle but both me and my partner had trouble swallowing this dish. I say avoid their water boiled section all together. This dish made both of us sick that night...

4 dishes was wayyyy too much food for 2 people and  we had enough for a second meal. but the bill for 4 dishes was 50$, now thats not too bad for a normal restaurant. But for flushing and a basement establishment I expect the bill for 2 people not exceeding 35... while going over the menu, alot of the items had increased prices, they just wrote the higher price over the older one. and all of their 'signature' dishes are 30$... wtf ? 
So why is this place overrated again?
New yorkers have a tendency to overrate hole in the wall places. It gives them a sense of accomplishment and entitlement for 'discovering' a restuarant not many people notices. but come on now... you are in flushing, theres just too many other fine places you can spend your money on instead of here.

The fact that I left with my lips on fire is always a good sign that the Sichuan restaurant is doing a good job. 

My recommendation is to bring someone who speaks Chinese with you. It was hard enough being a Chinese-American to read the menu and try to remember which dishes I like, but it helped a lot to ask my mom what Sichuan dishes are famous. Plus, the waitress pretty much only talked to me (the lone Asian in the crowd) because she assumed I was the only person who could speak Chinese. I'm just glad I can at least say dish names ha ha. 

Two dishes that my mom recommended that are famous are Mapo Tofu and Gan Bian Si Ji Dou. 

1. Mapo Tofu = spicy soft tofu in a spicy sauce ... I LOVED it, but my American friends didn't. I'm not sure what that tells you ... but this dish is probably one of my all-time favorites and I thought this restaurant did a decent job. 

2. Gan Bian Si Ji Dou = dry spicy fried green beans were EXCELLENT. This was probably the majority favorite. I think most people would look this over on the menu b/c who wants to eat green beans, but they are awesome.

We also ordered Kung Pao Chicken which was excellent. Very large portion and very spicy. The spicy fish stew was awesome and even spicier. And the lamb was the cherry on top to burn your face off. If you need to cool off, I would recommend the cold noodles and the chinese spinach. 

For 10 dishes and a beer or 2 for all 9 of us, we only paid about $15 each including tax and tip. I'd say that's a pretty good deal. I wouldn't pass this place up just because it's a little dinky and lacking with the A/C. I've decided the dirtier the restaurant, the better the food is. 

Just try it out and I think you'll leave satisfied.

Whoa.  WHOA.  First, let me say that I'm no Chinese food expert and am unfamiliar with what authentic Sichuan cuisine should taste like.  That being said, Little Pepper serves the best Chinese food I've ever had.  I'll admit that I was slightly apprehensive as I walked down into the basement space, but I had a feeling that I'd walk out very satisfied.  My gut was correct.   Everything I tried was incredibly flavorful and interesting.  I was sweating and sniffling from the copious amounts of spice, but it was never overwhelming and actually felt great.  Honestly, it was like I was on some sort of drug (if I find out the food was laced with crack, I'll be super pissed).  I know I sound certifiably insane, but I've gone here with two different people and both had the same exhilarating experience.  For starters, the bamboo shoots (soft but not mushy, in a pleasantly spicy sauce) and beef tendon (surprisingly appealing texture and a great, cool contrast to all the heat) are both excellent.  As for entrees, the absolute must have, in my humble opinion, is the lamb in hot and spicy sauce with cumin.  That shit is transcendental.  This is followed by an almost-as-good braised fish in spicy soup.  The portions are gargantuan and two starters and two mains are more than enough for two people and would probably be more appropriate for four.  The staff is warm and inviting despite some negative comments I've read.  I know Flushing is out of the way for many of you, but I promise it's worth the trip.  You can hop on the 7 or, if you drive, there are plenty of inexpensive public lots nearby.  Gather a few people and prepare for an amazing meal.

Little Pepper is yet another restaurant in the neighbourhood I've told myself to try, only to time and again succumb to my yearning for the food at other restaurants which I already know to be good. One Friday night I finally resolved to march my ass over there and have dinner. This restaurant is located in a very non-descript location with a relatively small amount of foot traffic for Flushing, and at the basement level, no less.  It's very easy to miss unless you were looking for it, but I actually get my hair cut every three or four weeks at a barber shop just a couple of doors from it, so I've took mental note of this restaurant for a while now.

Little Pepper is appropriately named since it serves Sichuan cuisine, which is known to be spicy. It was about 9 o'clock at night when I walked in, and it was clearly very busy inside. In fact, all the tables were occupied. The dining area was served by a middle aged woman and a young man who could be the woman's son and was probably drafted into working at the family business. Though I did not ask, so I could be wrong. This team of two was basically running around taking orders and fulfilling their requests without a second to even take a breath. They clearly needed to hire more people to work there on weekend nights. At various times the cooks even brought the dishes out from the kitchen and asked one of the waiters which table the dishes should go to. They have four or five small tables that can sit four people, and three big round tables. One of the big tables was only occupied by two people, and after about five minutes of waiting, I was finally sat down to share the big table with the party of two.

Now maybe it is boring of me, but everytime I go to a Sichuan restaurant, I order the Shui Zhu Niu - literally translated as "Water Cooked Beef". At Little Pepper, this dish is listed as Braised Beef in Spicy Soup Base. In one of my previous reviews of another restaurant in Flushing, I have described this very spicy dish of braised beef soaked in a big pot or bowl of peppery sauce. It is one of my favourite dishes and also the dish with which I measure how good or authentic a Sichuan restaurant is. I also noticed they have rabbit meat dishes and I had wanted to order the Diced Rabbit Meat in Red Chilli Sauce, which is listed as an appetiser on their menu. Unfortunately they were out of rabbit meat. Instead I settled on the Shredded Potato with Pickled Cabbage, which the people I was sharing the table with were eating and assured me was very good.

About ten minutes of waiting, the Shredded Potato with Pickled Cabbage was served. This is a simple dish of stir fried shredded potatos and pickled cabbage. The Chinese name of the dish indicated this should be a sour dish, but instead it was spicy. The potato itself was not spicy, however, it was the pickled cabbage that was spicy. Taking a bite of both the potato and the spicy pickled cabbage together made for a great contrast of flavours, though ultimately, this dish was not something that really stood out. The dish was not very spicy at all, it was only spicy enough to tingle your mouth. But I have a feeling that's how it was supposed to be. A little while later, the Shui Zhu Niu came out, and to my relief, they served it correctly with the beef literally swimming in a big bowl of spicy peppery sauce. I have been to other Sichuan restaurants where they do not do this, and only served the beef on a plate. They also had the spiciness level right, which was extremely spicy, to the point where you could feel the spiciness by simple contact of your tongue to the beef. The beef was also very tender as it ought to be. I was sweating embarassingly while eating this dish as I usually do when I eat very spicy dishes. At this point I was noticing that since the team of two waiters were so busy, some of the customers simply went to the cooler in the back of the dining area to get cold drinks for themselves. So I followed their lead and got up to get myself a cold bottle of Budweiser to soothe the spiciness in my mouth. In my opinion there is really very few eating experiences as enjoyable as eating a very spicy dish while drinking cold and bitter beer. It's a feeling that I can only describe as "tong kuai" in Chinese - I don't think there is a direct English translation for this phrase, but it describes a sort of carefree feeling of joy. It's a feeling that you might experience if you were driving down an empty highway in a convertible at 100 miles per hour, or if you were out partying with dear old friends till 4 in the morning without a hint of being tired, or if you were eating a very spicy dish with a cold beer to wash it down.

Came here on a late Sunday night for dinner.  Don't live in the area, but definitely a ways off from main street in a kinda sketchy neighborhood (right across from the projects).  This place is pretty unassuming since their restaurant is in the basement.  The owners are a husband and wife duo with the wife working the front of the house and the husband in back cooking.  Was welcomed right away by the wife as she warned me (in Mandarin) that there was only an hour left before they were going to close.  Being illiterate (or nearly so), I told her I wasn't sure how to say it but just pointed to a spicy fish and tofu dish on the menu.  The dish came out very quickly and just looking at it, I knew it was going to be spicy.  The plate was steaming and a nice red film of chili oil was floating on top.  The dish had cilantro on top, fish, tofu, and some peanuts.  It was pretty spicy and it tasted great.  After eating my bowl of rice, the woman asked "was it spicy enough for you?".  Obviously my face was red, a slight sweat going, nose running, and I'm sure my lips were a bit inflamed :).  Since it was closing time the husband came out from the kitchen and we chit chatted for awhile.  So overall?  Great service, prices are ok, and certainly authentic chinese food.

VERY SPICY just how I like it!  The blue crabs with hot pepper was so hot I was dripping sweat as I was picking for the meat.    The lamb in foil was good but oily.  I was not expecting it to taste like the $1 lamb skewers on the street but it did.. don't know if I would order it again.     Can't wait to try all the other goodie dishes.

Little Pepper has moved!  The new location is brighter, cleaner (not hard compared to the last place) and shinier, with a disconcertingly large amount of space between tables.  It's now at 18-24 College Point Blvd, a spot that is not convenient to any substantial public transportation, on a block chock full of generic Chinese takeout joints.    

The hostess and her staff are still as welcoming and lovely as can be and do their best to make sure you're having a great time. The food is good and spicy.  We've always liked their water braised beef and fish (the name is misleading, it doesn't prepare you for neon red broth and oil that accompanies the protein) and the dumplings, but our love for the hot pot was dampened by this last visit.  Instead of being able to order hot pot items a la carte when they were at their last location, you are given zero choice and two heaping plates of stuff you may or may not want.  We were of the latter sentiment.

But no matter, if you're in the area or are feeling adventuresome, check this place out.  It's worth the haul.

Note:  New Address for this killer Sichaun food temple-
18-24 College Point Blvd

Outstanding food and Nora, the hostess is incredibly helpful with her excellent English!

Fabulous appetizers included:  Thin sliced Beef tendon with Chili sauce - unbelievable; silken tofu with fresh scallion was just that;  fresh cucumber with mashed garlic sauce; spicy cold noodles.

Dishes we ate today:
Dried Sauteed String Beans - terrific, Fried Potato in Hot Sauce, Enhanced Pork with salt and pepper, braised lamb and beef in spicy soup base (menu category:  braised dishes), lamb in hot and spicy sauce (w. cumin)- lovely meatballs; house special griddle cooked rabbit and braised whole fish with spicy hot chili and scallion.

Bring a team and order extravagantly!  Balance spicy dishes with other dishes - we didn't and hence we ate rice to cool our palates down!

Spectacular Chinese food, no longer will I settle for anything less than Little Pepper.  Simply amazing and so incredibly inspired.  It's absolutely one of my favorite places to eat.  

The service is great, the hostess is very kind, friendly and helpful.  She informed me that the head chef began learning to cook when he was 15 years old and after 30 years experience he is one of my food heros.  

All of these dishes come highly recommended:
Appetizers: Dumplings in Hot Sauce, Sliced Pork Belly in Chili Garlic Sauce, and Pork Dan Dan Noodles.  

Main Courses: Peanut Chicken, Crust of Cooked Rice with Pork, Lamb with Cumin.

Went last night to reincarnation of Little Pepper and was  pleased with what I found. Location is way off beaten path of Flushing and at 9:00 pm it's kind of desolate. New digs are larger, cleaner, air conditioned and bright (too bright). Ordered Hot spicy cold noodles and porkbelly in a garlic hot oil brew.....delicious!!!! Lamb in spicy sauce with cumin was perfect as was the garlic crab. Despite any shortcomings we will be revisiting many times for our FIX! Tab for 2 $48
ADDENDUM: Returned 3/15 anticipating another great meal. Unfortunatly the cooking seems to have gone down hill. The only highlight was the poached pork in a spicy garlic sauce. The braised fish in red hot oil was good.The Cumin Lamb had an acedic taste and the Dan Dan noodles was nothing to crow about. Given that this place is out of the downtown Flushing area in College Point, I would go to another locale like Foo Run or Gran Szchuan or anyplace for that matter. Now that I think about it the taste was like chewing on aluminum foil...yuuucccchhhh!

So glad that they moved and not close.  I would've cried...

Been coming here for almost 4 years.  

Favorite Orders: Chicken Sichuan Style - crunchy, spicy, so good.  Shredded beef with peppers - spicy, tasty, juicy, and so damn good I could eat a whole plate.  Sauteed watercress - refreshing.

If I still lived in Queens, this would be my weekly go-to spot.  But this is a reason to go to Queens and enjoy fire in your mouth.

Although it's way out there for many bound by the (pretty) far reaches of the subway, you'll be rewarded with a roomy, light and airy dining room -- not commonplace for most Chinatown spots in my experience.

The garlic sauce is tasty and fits any cut of meat and, for the veggie crowd, eggplant just as well. Go for the kick of the spicy cold noodles. The shrimp with peanuts and hot peppers is also worth a mention.

$5.50-$6.50 lunch specials daily until 4, except Thursdays since it's closed.

Little pepper is a good little shinning star! I never would have known of this place if it wasn't for my friends looking for something new! Place is clean and roomy. The location is not the best in college point. I don't think I would ever cruise around there. But glad I did!

Won tong soup! How can that be WOW? Well how about if it's fresh! Simple? But not many place do such things! Yeah gross!!! But when you taste the food at little pepper you say "this is how it should be!". Sooo good! I wish I could do a drive by just for the soup but after tasting a variety of dishes I know I would end up getting more food than my hips need! Price is very good. Service friendly with a smile :0)
Stop by you will end up doing a few drive bys and actually stopping a few times.
The food was super spicy which I love, but also VERY salty and I could not finish it. I will have to try it another time in person and ask if there's any way to make it with less salt.

Review for General Tso Chicken, Chicken and brocoli and Tofu house style.

Okay, so went in for their lunch special which are on average 5.50 per dish. Not bad for price. Also, this place has Michelin rating. Interesting right? Also, each dish comes with rice. 

Well, General Tso, the portion was kind of small, maybe only 7 chunks of chicken came on. However, the sauce was delicious. Sweet and spicy. I scooped up the sauce on rice and ate it.  

Chicken and Brocoli was mostly Brocoli, but their sauce was delicious as well. mostly soy-sauce based taste, but it did have a little spicy peppery kick to it. 

Lastly, Tofu House style was extremely spicy. The tofu was thinly sliced, soft and limp. If you like tofu and like spicy, I highly recommend this dish. 

Personally, their rice seemed NON-CHINESE. It was more sticky, rather than the usual spread apart rice you get at other places. Also, our waiter barely spoke any english. I had to point to things on the menu and point at my empty rice bowl to indicate I wanted more rice.

So, Why is this 4 stars? The price is modest and the food was freshly made. The sauce was what got me to give them the high rating. The meat and the vegetable are about the same as other Chinese restaurants, but their sauce is delicious. I wish I had just ordered a bowl of their sauces and a large bowl of rice to dump them in...

I'm just ripping this off of my food blog.  The food at Little Pepper is absolutely delicious.  

Sliced Beef Tendon in Spicy Sauce
Cold, light, almost like an al dente pasta, salty and spicy.  My friend laughed, "It tastes like it has the same spices as the Burger King spicy chicken sandwich!"  Strangely enough, he was right... and it was a good thing.

Dan Dan Noodles
So. Freaking. Delicious.  We destroyed this dish and were tempted to drink the remaining fire broth.  But, we decided against it as we had four more dishes ahead of us.  I would go back just to eat this again. 

Lamb with Hot and Spicy Sauce (with Cumin)
This dish should've been called Cumin with Tender Lamb.  It was a bit overpowering but fragrant and so good.

Sizzling Rice with Fish
We were trying to be healthy! Actually, we were trying to alleviate some of the heat on our tastebuds.  The fish was perfectly cooked and the toasted rice in the neutralizing sauce and the vegetables were great!

Mapo Doufu
(Bean curd with spicy minced pork) I've made and/or consumed a considerable amount of mapo doufu in my lifetime.  It was a staple in my house growing up as my mother is not exactly a stellar cook... wait, I never said that. DELETE. DELETE. DELETE.

The tofu was so silky and smooth.  The sauce was complex and spot on.  I wanted to eat this and only this for the rest of the weekend but I started getting full... 

Shredded Tea-Smoked Duck with Ginger

If we weren't so completely full of beer (BYOB) and FIVE prior dishes, we would have eaten this whole plate.  Tea-smoked anything can go horribly wrong but this was really spectacular.  THE SMOKEY GOODNESS!

Overall, we had a great meal at Little Pepper.  I highly recommend it as the drive out to Queens is irrelevant when it comes to Sichuan cuisine of this caliber.  Service isn't quite there but if you're looking for Michelin-star quality, go see someone else.  The food is all there is here... and it's worth it.

Little Pepper is a jewel in College Point. Friendly staff, clean and well lit dining area, a large menu with so many options, and talented chefs. Try the scallion pancakes and spicy cold noodle. The only downside is the beer selection, last time I was there they only had Budweiser.

The food here is delicious but not for the faint of heart.  You better be able to handle the spice!  We always have to figure out what's the best dish to order for our daughter because she doesn't like spicy.  But so glad they opened a new location after they left Flushing.  Just wish it wasn't on College Point because it's a little aggravating trying to park here.  But the Dan Dan noodles are the best!  and I love the mapo tofu.  I was actually craving some today and don't know where I can even get anything comparable down here by the office!  Also, they mainly speak Mandarin, so at times it can be a little hard to communicate.  but they're still pretty nice there!
Very good and authentic Chinese food close to home.  I've been here often and have never been disapointed.  If they had delivery I would ne giving them a lot more business.

Little Pepper is sooooo freaking good.  I'm not sure if I know anything about Szechuan food, but what their cooking up in this restaurant tastes fantastic.  Whther for lunch or dinner the chef can handle a wok.  Everything comes our so balanced in flavor, not oily, and often smokey from the high heat.  

And the fact that I can go for lunch and eat for under $10 including tip is outrageous.  Every time I finish my lunch, which is about once a week, I can not imagine their is a finer plate of food at this price point anywhere in the five boroughs.

Standouts include the pork with bamboo shoots (I think it's fish fragrant pork), pork meatballs in garlic sauce, baby shrimp with peanuts and red chile, shredded beef with green pepper, wontons in spicy sauce, and any of the braised dishes.  Amen.

There aren't that many great restaurants in College Point which is further north from the Asian food-mecca that is Flushing, but Little Pepper is definitely one of the best restaurants in the entire area. Their cold appetizers are fantastic (especially the beef tendon) and super spicy. The peppery spices they use in all their foods are so fragrant and painfully good. One of the dishes that I HAVE to get there every time (if even just to take home) is the dan dan noodles! The noodles are super chewy and the sauce is fantastic.

If you order the stewed fish (or braised fish, I'm not sure what it's called in English), be warned that the portion is very large! Last time we went, we invited some friends, six of us total and we all loved it but still had to take home leftovers. 

I wish they'd deliver but I can understand the difficulty in transporting some of the dishes they serve. But one can dream...

If you're looking for some authentic Schezuan food in Queens and you don't want to deal with the traffic in Main St., this is the place to go. The food is delicious and it will leave your mouth wanting more even though your stomach is begging you to stop eating.
I'm coming back for sure!

I found this gem in College Point and it was awesome! 

First, it was much easier finding parking here versus Flushing. 

Upon entering Little Pepper we were promptly greeted. My wife and I ordered the Beef Tendon in chili sauce. It was excellent. Be warned, this is not a lean dish.

We also ordered the dumplings. They were fresh made and the sauce that they were served with was awesome! 

Our main course was the Mapo Dofu which was awesome as well. It was not what we expected but it turned out to be a wonderful, flavorful dish! 

Check it out!!

Little Pepper is not the small basement eatery it used to be. It has come out of its hiding place and is now a neat little restaurant on College Point Blvd. If you're taking public transportation like we did, you have to take a 10 minute bus ride on the Q65 from Main St. which isn't bad at all since it comes every 12 minutes. I came here in a group of 3 on a Saturday around 2pm and it was empty.  The interior is simple but nice and has plenty of space. We got:

Sliced Beef Tendon w/ Chili Sauce -  We get this dish in every Sichuan place we go to. I liked theirs a lot as it had good flavor and texture throughout.  4/5 http://www.yelp.com/user_local_photos?select=oOuL3MBEZ5V7ltEwt7LPAA&userid=33h9Jv4VKbbxB42CUD9WQg

Lamb with Hot & Spicy Sauce (w. Cumin) - Decent flavor but lamb was a little dry and they used more onions than necessary. Wasn't as spicy as I expected. The Muslim Lamb Chops at Fu Run remains my favorite cumin lamb dish. 3.5/5 http://www.yelp.com/user_local_photos?select=hLs-gvfPzzjNwv0wjQHOcQ&userid=33h9Jv4VKbbxB42CUD9WQg

Braised Sliced Fish in Spicy Soup Base - Best & spiciest dish of the night.  They have this dish listed twice.  Under "Seafood", it's $40 whereas under the "Braised Dishes" section it's $15. I think they use fresh fish for the "Seafood" dish whereas the one we ordered was frozen fish. You can't go wrong ordering the $15 version like us.  5/5 http://www.yelp.com/user_local_photos?select=WI9nvLynJ-2UgSkc-AONhA&userid=33h9Jv4VKbbxB42CUD9WQg

Spicy Cold Noodle -  My friend wanted to have something cold and dry to balance out all the heat and oil. Not sure if this was the best dish for that purpose but it wasn't too bad. 3/5 http://www.yelp.com/user_local_photos?select=KtwNrh8e4uJ8EZEYASzlOw&userid=33h9Jv4VKbbxB42CUD9WQg

Dumpling in Hot Sauce - This came out looking like a superstar but the dumplings were bland. 2/5 http://www.yelp.com/user_local_photos?select=bgZZIije_5p0jIeQA-kk9g&userid=33h9Jv4VKbbxB42CUD9WQg

Mapo Tofu -  I was happy to see that they do my favorite Sichuan dish well here. Good amount of heat, silky tofu and peppercorns nicely rounded up the flavors. 4/5 http://www.yelp.com/user_local_photos?select=hrgntRbIsngn0YRyGAclIA&userid=33h9Jv4VKbbxB42CUD9WQg

They dumbed down the spice for us since my wife isn't big on spice. It was still very spicy for her and she had to walk out during the meal and get a quart of milk from a nearby grocery store. On the other hand, I could've used more spice in all the dishes. 

Their presentation was impressive- all the dishes looked good when they came out. Most lived up to our expectations. The service was fine. Since we were just about the only table in the restaurant, we got their attention very quickly even though they seemed engrossed by what looked like the Chinese version of "The Voice" on TV.

This is an ideal place to come in a group if you are interested in exploring the Flushing food scene as it's off Main St. and you can enjoy your meal in relative peace. We took over two hours to finish our lunch.  It's easily accessible by public transportation and even though it might take some time to get here, the food is worth it.

Thanks for the heads up on the move, fellow yelpers. I went to their old location last year and saw the gates down. I began to cry a bit because I thought they closed down for good. Little Pepper is one of the best Szechuan places I've eaten in and one of the oldest. It's also the first in Flushing. I remember my mom taking me here after ballet class at the Y when I was 8. Now I take my husband here. The prices are fair, and the food is deeelicious! Our favorite is the spicy fried pork with szechuan peppercorn that alters the taste of everything you eat. It's so freaky good!
Flushing food with out the Flushing headache.  Parking spots all over without the traffic.  Food is hella good too.  Everything I've ordered here has been fantastic.

Their food is awesome. I've been here with my boyfriend a couple of times, and I would say this is one of the best Chinese restaurants I've been to. The food is uncomfortably spicy, but delicious! It's one of those restaurants where you can taste the spiciness without the spicy having to kill the taste of the actual food if you know what I mean. 

Most of the dishes we ordered were from the lunch special and is spicy except for the duck. Here's what I recommend: 

Smoked Tea Duck: 4/5 stars. Tastes pretty good, but it isn't the kind of food you can't find in other restaurants. On the pricey side ($15). 

Chinese chicken nugget: 4.2/5 stars. I didn't know Chinese made chicken nuggets till my visit to Little Pepper. Sounds like take out food, but it isn't. Just picture chicken from an order of General Tso's Chicken, except it's bigger, crispier, with a different sauce over it. I'm happy it wasn't a McDonald's white meat chicken nugget on a plate. 

Chicken with peanuts: 4.5/5 stars. It was diced chicken mixed with peanuts in a light brown sauce.

Shredded beef with pepper: 4.2/5 stars. Probably the most spicy dish we have ordered in Little Pepper. 

Chinese meatballs: 4.5/5 stars. Sounds strange, considering that I never knew Chinese made meatballs. Was worried that I would order Chinese take out food, but turned out to be just as authentic as the other dishes I have ordered. The dark brown sauce is delicious. 

Spicy cold noodles: 5/5 stars. Like what the name says. The dish has a strong peanut smell and taste to it. 

Dumplings: 4.8/5 stars. I don't like that the dish is kind of oily, but because of the taste, it's a must have when you're in little pepper. 

Service is good. Atmosphere is clean and simple. Nothing to complain about.

We ordered three dishes.. mapo tofu, dan dan noodles, and stir-fired dou miao (vegetables).  Everything was fantastic. The spice was just right.  Mostly, I was impressed by how fresh the vegetables were!  Can't wait to come back and try more dishes.

Little Pepper is fantastic. The food is wonderful, and the prices are affordable. It's small, but there are always tables available. Every dish I've tried has been delicious, and in the year I've been visiting I haven't had a single bad experience. Highly recommended.

Vibe: The vibe of the restaurant is totally different from their old location across from the Bland Houses in Flushing. The interior is clean, bright and the service is no-nonsense friendly. I usually go during lunch and the restaurant always has ample seating so you can go and not feel rushed by yourself or with a group during a weekday lunch. 

Location and Parking:
The new restaurant is located on a busy commercial stretch of College Point Blvd. Street muni-meter parking or free parking on some of the back side streets can be found. 

Food:
You can't go wrong with Mapo-tofu, beef with green pepper, wontons in spicy oil, dandan noodles. Pretty much everything I've tried here is accessible and delicious. The food is humble and sometimes can be a little too greasy (drink lots of tea). But it tastes fresh and if you are looking for spicy mouth numbing sichuan peppercorn packed food try a bunch of dishes and enjoy!

Quite possibly the best Chinese food that I've had in this city! 

Although located way out in the boonies of north College Point, past the gritty stretch of industrial buildings to the east of LaGuardia - it is well worth the trek! The space is very clean and bright with interesting artwork, including a painting of a storm trooper and wrapped chocolate truffles. 

The menu is quite large and if you choose wisely, you can build a diverse and affordable meal - particularly if you go with a larger crowd (highly recommended!) Given the multitude of choices, we opted to go for a bit of everything. 

The signature Braised Sliced Fish in a Spicy Soup Broth was excellent (opt for the $15 version tucked away under the "braised dishes" section. The Dan Dan noodles with pork were awesome...such an explosion of flavor and I could detect a nice bit of anise in there. The scallion pancakes were your standard fare, but the star of the dish is the delicate sweet sauce that is served with it - far from your standard soy or dumpling sauce mixed with scallion. 

We also tried the pickled cow pea with pork - a very curious and interesting dish, although to be forewarned: it does have quite the odor! If you can deal with it, it is worth a try. The smoked duck with ginger was also quite good...very light and served with onions and peppers - big plus for not having to deal with bones! 

The 4.5 average rating is well deserved and I highly recommend trooping it out here - you won't regret it!

Used to love this place, but recently got so disappointed~ ordered a braised sliced beef in spicy soup base for a party about ten people, but it is even not enough for each of us to get a slice!!! This is not the first time!!! It is totally no sense!!! And the taste is not as good as before either. The dish is $17 including tax, and the amount is so small. Need a careful consideration before you order something for take out

4.5 stars.

As some have said, this could be the best Chinese food in NYC. Forget Mission Chinese in Mnahattan, get to this place.   Went with a party of 4 and we got a bunch of dishes to share.  Everything was delicious, but the standouts were the beef with scallions (so flavorful and full of spice), the spicy squid was ridiculously good.  The Dan dan noodles were unbelievable.  The scallion pancakes were perfectly cooked, just crispy and also doughy enough to soak up the dipping sauce that came with it.  The spicy string bean app was so tasty that I couldn't believe that I was eating string beans.

Everything here is perfectly cooked and tastes delicious...definitely make sure you like some heat before coming here as they are not shy about it.

We brought beer as we thought it was BYOB... turns out they recently got a liquor license but they let us drink our beer anyway... how cool is that??

Would be 5 stars but the actual space leaves a bit to be desired.

My friends and I came here for hotpot and it was sooooo good. Hotpot isn't all you can eat, quality and selection of food seems extensive (I'm not a hotpot connoisseur) we got the half and half broth, spicy and non spicy. The broths tasted authentic and should be since both of my friends I ate with are from China and werent complaining. The spicy broth was hot (temperature and taste) and filled with tons of chili peppers- the two friends I was with were sweating, coughing and needed constant cold water refills, so eat slow! Sauce station-  pretty standard, your usual cilantro, soy and sesame sauce. Cash only! Four stars for good food, service and cleanliness!

Great authentic sichuanese food.  Two dishes definitely stood out from the 8 dishes that we ordered:  The sliced fish with hot pepper is amazing.  It tasted like fish flavored butter in hot pepper oil.  Sliced pork belly was succulent and full of garlic (no kissing for 24 hours after consumption, but I would eat this every hour of every day) The place is far from public transportation, so it is not as crowded as other sichuanese restaurant in Flushing.

We were three total and ordered 8 mains. All were spectacular -- the double cooked pork was amongst the best versions I've ever had of this dish. Chonqing chicken, the scary-but-delicious looking mound of peppers and poultry, was equally as outstanding. The one slight downer was the cumin beef (traditionally with lamb, but one of the guys frowned upon lamb we were eating with), which was perfectly fine but not as stellar as some of the crispier, more cuminy versions we've had elsewhere (Sichuan Gourmet in midtown Manhattan has the best I've had of this dish). The tea smoked duck was truly great, but missing its plum sauce of all things. It's not that they forgot it -- they just don't serve it with it or have any in the restaurant at all!  And it desperately needed it to round out its otherwise solid flavor and crispiness. The sliced fish in hot bean paste is superb and original, but order it with a side of rice. It's unbelievable. One last thing: this place ain't easy to get to. It's not an easy subway ride away. The LIRR is better to Flushing, but then you have to catch a bus to College Point. So, plan accordingly, bring friends and make a day in Flushing out of it. Be warned, however: it's randomly closed on Thursdays!  The first time we attempted a trip here, we found this out the hard way.
this place is seriously authentic and super tasty. you better enjoy spicy food (like me) or you are in trouble!

Been going here since it opened.  A man and woman own and run it.  CASH, only.  Used to be REALLY good.  If you get your food to go, the servings will be about half the size of dining-in portions.  They used to be perfect:  food quality, portions, service.  Now they are cutting corners.  Bad economy?  Apathy?  About a year ago, I bought four dishes to go, spent $60, plus tip, and when I got home I noticed the owner charged me an extra $10.  I was charged $15.95 for a $5.95 noodle dish.  I should have reviewed the check when I payed but I trusted him since I had been there so many times.  (He sure was happy when I gave him all that cash!  Now I know why!)  Too inconsistent to keep my business.

Went to the Little Pepper with the family.  I think they still have one in Flushing... anyway, I'm not the biggest fan of this type of food but food is food and deserves a fair shot.

We started with the fresh cucumbers w/ garlic (can't really mess that up) and the scallion pancakes.  I wholeheartedly recommend everyone get the scallion pancakes from this place.  The dipping sauce was some soy sauce concoction with some maybe peanut type sauce in it?  It took a lot of will power not to drink the sauce.  Anyway, the sauce and the perfectly fried scallion pancakes - what a balance.  

They have this Dan Dan noodle.  Totally delicious and less oily than the other dishes.  Great flavor.  Must try.

For my main I got the pork meatballs in garlic sauce.  The meatball is homemade.  The garlic sauce was great with rice.  The meatballs were ok.  Mapo tofu was too oily... I guess it's always coated in oil but I was not a fan of the sauce used.  I really do miss the Szechuan Capital from waaaaaay back in the day... they made the best mapo tofu.  I digress.  To cut all the oil and spice, we got some veggie dish that was pretty standard.  I think it was a gourd....

BTW - if you enjoy challenges while eating, do try the chicken in sichuan style.  It was kind of like navigating through a landmine (though I've never navigated through a landmine so maybe I shouldn't have used that example)....  the chicken pieces were about the same size as the chili pieces and coated with these pepper corns.  I was doing a pretty good job of avoiding the chilis and peppercorn but missed one.  I bit into the pepper corn, looked at my brother and said "oh that wasn't too bad."  His response was "waaaaait for it."  My tongue went numb.  What a weird feeling... =-\

I was recommend by a friend who was from Sichun. The food was excellent, we came here almost once a month since the first time, that is not a easy thing to pay two bridges toll. I love the hot fish pot, very spicy, but so delicious. Also loved the pine nut with corn, if you can not handle very spicy food, this dish is a good one to start, it is easy one to copy at home also. The cold noodle, the spicy wonton, string bean, eggplant..... , too many dishes, to little stomach.

Excellent Sichuan food and warm friendly service. Not too far out of the way, only five minutes from the Whitestone. We went at lunchtime so it was quiet.
Definitely worth the trip , we had the ox lung in chili sauce to start followed by the spicy lamb with cumin and the shredded tea smoked duck and ginger.

We used to eat at Xiao Lajiao all the time when it was still in that basement space in Flushing, and we loved it. Not haute Sichuan cuisine, but the kind of food that you might eat in the restaurant around the corner in a working class neighborhood in Chengdu. 

Visiting again after a fairly long time, I'm relieved to find the food hasn't changed. The old formula still applies: the wife looks after the cash register, while the husband manages the kitchen and their son's corny artwork adorns the walls. 

I preferred the dingy but cozy atmosphere of that basement to this garishly lit and empty-looking new space. Plus this location sucks; no reason to hang out on this stretch of College Point Blvd unless you live nearby. And the prices, never low to begin with, have been creeping up. 

Still, when we want Chinese comfort food, this is the first place we think of.

It's probably not mentally healthy, the extent to which Little Pepper invades my thoughts.  I pine for Little Pepper's affordable, abundant, and skilled use of that numbing Szechuan peppercorn.   I daydream about their near-perfect vanishing point of sweet and savory that is the homeade jerky appetizer.  Their lamb with cumin is the best version of this dish I've tasted in this city.  I love the intense heat of their bamboo shoot appetizer, the insane punch of numbing spice in their braised fish, and do not miss out on the best thing to ever happen to french fried potatoes:  Szechuan peppercorns and cumin.  

We get out here at least once a month by car, and it's never enough.

Wow.  I can't believe I haven't posted about this place for years.  I guess part of the reason for that is that I don't get there as often as I'd like or as often as it deserves.  Little Pepper used to be located on a slightly dingy strip of Roosevelt Ave. in Flushing.  A few years ago they moved to a much nicer space in College Point.  Unfortunately even with a car the place is something of a haul from my apartment in Brooklyn.  

I need to say this up front - I think Little Pepper is serving some of the best Sichuan food you can get in New York.  I'd rank it up there with Lan Sheng.  Yes, it's that good.

The new digs fall on the higher end of "bright lights Chinese."  Everything is sparkly clean and new.

http://farm8.staticflickr.com/7106/7081825997_01d73c5ba7_z.jpg

http://farm6.staticflickr.com/5117/6935753682_488ef61609_z.jpg

We've probably been to the new venue 5 or 6 times.  I should have posted about my meals while the memory was fresh but oh well.

Dan Dan noodles.

http://farm9.staticflickr.com/8306/7884386690_20017e2351_z.jpg

I think their version is the best in the city.  Not as saucy as some but there's plenty of Sichuan peppercorns hiding in that bowl.  For some reason most Sichuan restaurants serve their noodles in ridiculously small bowls which make it a real trick to toss the noodles and cover them in sauce.  At LP the bowls are larger and noodles are already tossed when the bowl hit the table.  It would be great if this catches on.

Five Spiced Beef

http://farm8.staticflickr.com/7124/7081828827_40634b7d17_z.jpg

This is a ridiculously large portion, better suited for sharing with a group of six.  Not that I'm complaining.  The flavor is quite good if a bit one dimensional.  That's the nature of the dish.  You have 5 or 6 slices and move on.

Lamb with scallions.

http://farm8.staticflickr.com/7189/6935753068_af9d9b3b33_z.jpg

The name says it all.  It's tender and lamby and the scallions are the perfect pairing.  If you like lamb you need to order this.  Not overly spicy but still full flavored.

Chicken with Peanuts

http://farm8.staticflickr.com/7077/7081829165_d1e03c8819_z.jpg

I think this was everybody's gateway dish for Sichuan cuisine and over time you sort of graduate out of ordering it.  LP's version reminds you of why you liked it in the first place.  There's plenty of heat and the chicken is suitably juicy.

Enhanced Pork.

http://farm8.staticflickr.com/7227/7081827615_a686541ea8_z.jpg

Our old friend who  we first met at Spicy & Tasty more than 10 years ago.  LP's version is top notch.  Another picture of the pork taken on a different day because I like looking at it.

http://farm8.staticflickr.com/7133/7081829921_01f503f55c_z.jpg

Beef w. Hot  Spicy Sauce w. Cumin

http://farm9.staticflickr.com/8322/7884384080_31c33c946b_z.jpg

For reasons unknown it's all wrapped up like a baked potato in a 1960s restaurant.  The flavor was wonderful though, plenty of cumin and nice and juicy.  Cumin is one of those spices that's easy to overuse.  LP's version of this dish keeps things in proportion.  (We've only had this once - I don't know if the aluminum wrapping was a one off or not.)

OK, we're up to last Sunday's meal.

Fresh Cucumber with mashed garlic sauce.

http://farm4.staticflickr.com/3794/9201823882_079f7c8c99_z.jpg

This was wonderful.  WONDERFUL.  The best version of this dish I've ever had.  It's served with plenty of lightly sauteed garlic which is a perfect counterpoint to the sesame oil dressing.  Not spicy at all but wonderfully refreshing.

Chicken Nuggets in Garlic Sauce

http://farm4.staticflickr.com/3732/9199044971_a865211545_z.jpg

My GF thought she was ordering a drier chicken presentation and the sauciness of this dish was a bit of an unpleasant surprise.  I think it was an issue of expectations.  There was a bit of sweet and sourness to the sauce with a good amount of underlying heat.  Pleasantly juicy.  I'd give it a B+ but my GF would probably grade it a B.

Wonton in Hot & Sour Sauce

http://farm6.staticflickr.com/5542/9199044873_f5c890743e.jpg

This picture is smaller for a reason.  It's only here as a warning.  While the wontons were generously sized and quite meaty the sauce was truly lackluster.  Slightly hot and sour, watery, and under salted.  Perhaps the kitchen was having a bad day on just this one dish?  Because everything else was wonderful.

I saved the best for last.  Sliced Pork with Tree Mushroom.

http://farm9.staticflickr.com/8035/7884385714_c2cf51940a_z.jpg

I struggle not to order this every time I go to Little Pepper.  The mushrooms are a great match to the pork and the sauce is slightly vinegary with a touch of sweetness and heat.  Complex and perfect.

I wish this restaurant was closer to me.  It really is that good.

http://farm8.staticflickr.com/7278/6935753440_d232a03df9_z.jpg
Dishes were authentic and enjoyably spicy. It's kind of far off from flushing, but a good place nonetheless. I love that spicy pork belly.

A good Chinese restaurant... with easy parking!? It can't be! 

But it is! Seriously, parking here is a breeze. I've been a few times and there is always a spot right in front. 

Little Pepper serves up some delicious meals and for those of you with family/friends who aren't fond of the dive-y food of Flushing, this place has food for them, too! Interior is nice with some cool paintings on the wall, though if you're trying to have a conversation, the blaring Chinese dramas might distract you when sudden cries of anguish break out behind you. I don't really mind, but one of my dining partners was going nuts. 

Mapo Tofu - I haven't had this for awhile, but I remember it being good with the fiery burn of Szechuan packed into this big plate of tofu. I haven't really been tempted to try it again despite the quality because there is just too much to try.

Two different shrimp dishes off the lunch special were pretty good. One was with peanuts, but I forget the name. Either way, the shrimp are nice and fresh and they're pretty good. Good for those people who want something a little closer to American-Chinese, minus the breading! Actually, good for anybody. It's pretty cheap!

Dan dan noodles - Mmmm. Yummy. Big fan. If you're in the moodle for some noodles, get these. If you aren't, get them anyway. 

Cucumber with garlic - Must try! Don't go on a date afterwards. 

Chicken Chongqing style has become a standby for my takeout after long workdays. Small bits of crispy chicken served with an equal amount of Szechuan peppers. Well worth a try if you're fan of the mala feeling of Szechuan peppers.

Pickled cowpea was a big hit, even with my somewhat conservative eater of a grandmother. Basically sliced up stir fried string beans with a nice tang to them.

First, about food: We have been there a few times, the spicy food are good, such a MaiPo Tufu, and Chung Qing spicy chicken. It is compatiable to the food such as the land of plenty in the city. Price is reasonable. Street parking is easy. 

Service is fast. However, Vegetable dish is lacking. I have ordered fried Chinese water spinach vegetable, It is in fact a mix of yellowish green, and normal looking green.  It is probably due the fact they mix left over vege and fresh vege together.  I can't understand why they want to ruin their good reputation in Yelp in order to make a few bucks.  

Now, here is the really bad part about this place: The waiters have to hand out their tip to the owner in this place.  I don't know how much the servers get paid, it is against the law to take the tip from the waiter by the owner, not to mention it is morally wrong on so many different levels. 

If you treat your waiters so bad, how can you expect the waiter provides good service.

I guess the owner still is in survival mood, here is a a tip for the owner: you have a nice, little restaurant with some good reviews about your food, don't ruin it! Otherwise, it won't last long in NYC.

Queue the angels.... 
Yes, QUEUE them! Tell them to get behind me on the line to Little Pepper! The night we went with 10 friends was one of the best eating experiences I've had this year.. Most memorable was the fish with bean curd and the cold noodles. So much so that I might be tempted to do something I rarely do and order it a second time. Everything I had was great and the staff was super nice. 

The menu is huge, but it seems like it would be hard to choose wrong. The place was clean and the art was probably the most legitimate I have seen in a restaurant. If I were to do it again, I'd try the scallion rice and bring 10 friends again.

I love this place. Such a great little restaurant, affordable and large portions of food. They are really kind serving us "welcomely" plus I love there lunch special. It's yummalicious! Such a great place in college point, and it's my favorite Chinese restaurant to eat at. Just as the name says, it mostly serves spicy dishes so if u crave something saucy and spicy, little pepper is where it's at.

4.5 stars.

I have taken quite a liking to Little Pepper. Szechuan food is simply ideal on a breezy or cold night. The heat from the dishes really warm you up after a bite!

So far, I have noticed that the servers are very kind and lighthearted, even though their English is just acceptable.

Always get the sliced pork belly in chili-garlic sauce. The menu says it's extra hot and spicy but I find it mild and even sweet. I also like the fish in spicy sauce. Be warned that it is a large dish! The fish is super tender and soft. As far as veggies go, my favorites are snow pea leaves and water spinach.

The only thing I wouldn't order again is the shrimp dish. I didn't think it was worth paying almost $15 for 10 shrimp swallowed up in chopped chili peppers. Other than that, the prices are very reasonable and comparable to most Chinese restaurants in Flushing. (My other favorite Szechuan restaurant is located there: Fu Run on Prince St.)

The restaurant is simple, clean and never too busy. Definitely give Little Pepper a try if you are in the area!
Love this place.  Delicious Szechuan!  Chung Qing chicken is amazing.  Also Cumin Lamb, Szechuan Fish, and crispy dry string beans all recommended.
A bit out of the way in College Point but the food was tasty.  We had the dan dan noodles, shredded potatoes, and spicy lamb.  Atmosphere is not the best but could be good for take out too.

Little Pepper is the best Szechuan restaurant in Flushing I have tasted so far. Their food are authentic Chinese flavor, and the price are reasonable.

The environment is simple and clean, with decor on walls drawn by the owner's son. The owner is lighthearted,friendly and informative, he shared the recipe of some dishes, which turned to be helpful when we cooked at home.

One thing I have to mention is that, I wouldn't recommend any "pot" food here, like shrimp pot or something like that I forgot the names. Those food come with a large portion of side dishes like chili peppers and potatoes, I don't think they are worth the money.

I'd strongly recommend here for anyone who fancies authentic spicy Szechuan food.

On the money this restaurant. One of the best Sichuan Restaurants that I've had this year (2013). It was no frills, very simple and straight forward. No iced carved buddha's or girls dressed up in Hanboks trying to seduce you to buying overpriced shots of patron mixed in kumquats.

The Shrimp with hot chili Oil is just orgy in your mouth. Btw.

Came here for lunch. We are always looking for Szechuan restaurants, and Little Pepper while just off the beaten path of Main Street Flushing fits the bill nicely.

The staff are very friendly, the place is very clean and sanitary.

We ordered the pickled szechuan cabbage which was one the best I've ever tried, although it was a little bit too oily. 

The ma-po tofu was great, although the portion could have been slightly bigger, and less oily. 

They have the best white rice here, for whatever reason. They use a little bit of oil, but it's cooked perfectly and sticks together nicely. 

Overall worth the trip to College Point.

It's as good as if not better than most of the places in downtown Flushing, but you wont feel all cramped up because it's not a little hole in the wall.

Came here once to eat-in and twice for take out, if you're looking for a good Szechuan restaurant, this one hits the money! Good food, excellent service (Friendly staff) and the restaurant itself is beautifully decorated. 

HIGHLY RECOMMENDED! 5 STARS

I don't get the hype. At all.

I'm a FIEND for authentic Sichuan. After a trip to Asia last month, I came home desperate to track down the most authentic and freshest Sichuan I could find in NYC. I read articles and forums and blogs and expected Little Pepper to be the holy grail. Finally made it with my boyfriend tonight and after trying many different dishes we both left merely satisfied. Definitely not blown away, and actually not even impressed. The most disappointing thing about Little Pepper was their under use of Sichuan peppercorn. Every single dish lacked the signature Sichuan peppercorn tang (it's not actually a peppercorn - it's part of the citrus family) and didn't deliver anything beyond a hint of tingling numbness. 

Garlic cucumbers - solidly good

Wonton in hot and sour sauce - ok, broth was overly sour and under salted and not really hot at all save for a small drizzle of chili oil 

Dan Dan Noodle - poor. flavorless noodles served in a watery sauce with not enough meat and nowhere near enough heat / tingling.

Bean Thread Noodle in Hot and Sour Soup - ehhhh big disappointment - hot and sour potato noodle soup loaded with sichuan peppercorn and fresh cilantro, peanuts and mung beans boiled in hot and sour broth with flavorful, chewy potato noodles is my favorite food on earth. I've been desperate to get ahold of an approximation stateside and this was such a miss. The thin bean curd noodles noodles were cooked in water and dumped into the broth just before being served - at first they had absolutely no flavor whatsoever. They did eventually soak up all of the broth, which I wasn't happy about, but at that point the flavor definitely improved in a serious way. The bean sprouts this was served with had an awful chloriney taste that totally distracted from enjoying it at all. No cilantro. No fresh herbs. Just chloriney sprouts and peanuts boiled in water with no flavor for garnish. SERIOUSLY lacking in heat / tingle. And a little too heavy on the sour without enough salt and heat to round it out. REALLY lacking on Sichuan peppercorn flavor, too, not just tingle.

Tea Smoked Duck - solidly good, great crispy skin (they actually fry it and serve it warm here) and the right fat to meat ratio

Ma Po Tofu - good but REALLY lacked on the mala heat / tingling and almost NO Sichuan peppercorn flavor at all...

I wanted to love Little Pepper. Especially because the service was so great and the prices reasonable. But I just didn't. At all. For me, Sichuan food is about an explosion of spices, aromas and sensations and this just didn't deliver the goods. The flavor and spice profiles weren't nuanced enough and the chili heat and Sichuan peppercorn tingling and signature flavor and aroma was really lacking across all of the dishes.

From what I've had, only Chengdu Heaven (Cheng Du Tian Fu) stands out as truly amazing as far as Sichuan food in NYC goes. Sichuan lovers looking for the best food in NYC should head there.

The staff is extremely friendly and great!

Food: 
Cucumbers                             B
Pork Belly in Spicy                  A
DanDan noodles                   B+ Ash is in a lot of the cooking. Ash = Kinda spice or hot spice that nums your mouth. 
Double cooked pork              A
Chicken with spicy peppers A A lot of Ash and peppers. 
Corn and Pine nuts               B
Few other entrees I do not remember B+, A

I love spicy food and this is a great place to outside of Flushing. Worth it.

I tried this place based on Yelp reviews and it's my favorite Chinese restaurant now.  I've been there 3 times and each time sampled 4-5 dishes and ordered some to go so I've had about 25% of the menu.  This is the least greasy/oily of all the Chinese restaurants I have tried in Flushing.  I don't remember Chinese food being so oily when I was growing up. I'm not sure whether I just wasn't aware of all the oil or if this is a new trend.

My two favorite dishes that I get each time are:

Cold sesame noodles & sauteed lotus root.  The cold sesame noodles are a delicious combination and balance of slightly sweet, slightly tangy, slighly nutty (sesame),  slightly peppery noodles in chili oil. The combination is delicious. I have tried sesame noodles in other Sz restaurants and they were boring, too mushy, or too oily or too single flavored, compared to the way Little Pepper makes them.  They are delicious here.

Sauteed lotus root was an experiment - I loved them.  They look wierd --like thin sliced potatoes with 5 holes in the middle. The texture is a little crunchy, a little soft like  sliced water chestnuts.  They are  sauteed with scallions, some szechuan pepper flakes, maybe garlic,  in a small amount of slightly thickened whitish sauce. They are best hot straight from the pan and don't taste as good for takeout or reheating at home. The waitress told me that the key is getting good lotus roots and the chef knows how to pick them. The dish is very mild but I liked the unusual texture and flavor.(And Lotus root is supposed to be cleansing for your liver, so eat up!).

One visit I ordered the lamb with spicy sauce (online menu -- it's called something else on the takeout menu and something else in the restaurant menu)  It has a lot of cumin in it and I've tried both lamb and beef. Lamb was the clear winner.  It was delicious and spicy -- has a lot of SzP in it. It goes well over rice. I found you have to ask for the rice -- they don't serve it unasked.

--I love hot & sour soup. Here It was sour without the depth of flavors of the hot & sour soup from Spicy & Tasty. Would not order it again.

--Cilantro meat ball with winter melon was good. The meatballs have the texture of small matzo balls and the wintermelon in the soup was an interesting texture combination. The melon didn't have much flavor. The soup was very mild but good. The texture of the melon in the soup was a little strange but the flavor was good.

-- mapo tofu was good -very spicy & swimming in too much red oil

--scallion pancake was less greasy and more crunchy than other places and dipping sauce was SUPERB - sweet and salty with Sz peppers. 

--Szechuan pickled cowpeas was Ok but not interesting--  I wouldn't order it again 

--sauteed pine nut and corn was just plain bad. It looked like canned corn that had been over sauteed. The corn was chewy and there were only a couple of pine nuts and maybe scallions sauteed with Sz peppercorns and maybe some other ingredients.  Would not recommend this dish.

-- sauteed string beans were delicious but somewhat over salted. Would still order them again but ask for little/no salt.

-- smoked tea duck szechuan style was tasty but there were so many bones & so little meat on each bone I wouldn't get it again.
